--- ## title: "Converted Presentation" format: revealjs: theme: default pagetitle: 'Stochastic Population Models' slide-number: true css: ../../custom.css lang: en --- # Introduction {visibility="hidden"} ## {content-align="center" style="font-size: 160%;"}
Stochastic Population Models
![](figs/pelagic-cormorants.png){height="3.5in"} ![](figs/kittiwakes.png){height="3.5in"}
## Today in APD ::: {style="font-size: 120%;"}
Random variables
Environmental stochasticity
Demographic stochasticity ::: ## Random variables ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} A random variable is a variable whose value can't be predicted with certainty.
::: {.fragment} Examples * Weather * Our own behavior * Population size ::: :::
::: {.fragment style="color: SeaGreen;"}
**Is the universe random? Or is just too complex to be predicted with certainty?**
::: ## Probability distributions A random variable ($X$) can be described by a probability distribution.
There are many types of probability distributions, including: * Normal (or Gaussian) * Poisson * Binomial * Multinomial ## Normal (Gaussian) Distribution ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} $$ X \sim \mbox{Normal}(\mu=0, \sigma^2=1) $$ :::
::: {.r-stack} ::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/norm-1) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/norm-2) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/norm-3) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/norm-4) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/norm-5) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=5} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/norm-6) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=6} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/norm-7) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=7} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/norm-8) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=8} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/norm-9) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=9} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/norm-10) ::: :::
## Normal (Gaussian) distribution ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/normals-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## A purely stochastic model ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} $$ N_t \sim \mbox{Normal}(\mu=50, \sigma^2=1) $$ ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/normpop-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Two important types of stochasticity ::: {style='font-size: 90%;'} **Environmental stochasticity** * Random variation in demographic rates (such as birth and death rates). * Caused by unpredictable changes (e.g., in weather, habitat, ... conditions) among years.
::: {.fragment} **Demographic stochasticity** * Random variation in demographic outcomes (such as the number of births and deaths). * Occurs even when demographic rates are constant. ::: ::: # Environmental stochasticity {visibility="hidden"} ## Geometric growth with env. stochasticity ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} $$ N_{t+1} = N_t + N_t r_t $$ $$ r_t \sim \mbox{Normal}(\bar{r}, \sigma^2) $$ ::: R code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nYears <- 20 N <- r <- rep(NA, nYears) ## Create empty N and r N[1] <- 100 ## Initial value of N r.bar <- 0.5 ## Average growth rate sigma <- 0.1 ## StdDev of growth rate for(t in 2:nYears) { r[t-1] <- rnorm(n=1, mean=r.bar, sd=sigma) N[t] <- N[t-1] + N[t-1]*r[t-1] } ``` ::: ## Geometric growth with env. stochasticity ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} $$ r_t \sim \mbox{Normal}(\bar{r}=0.1, \sigma^2=0.01) $$ ::: ::: {.cell} :::
::: {.r-stack} ::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex-1) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex-2) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex-3) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex-4) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex-5) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=5} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex-6) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=6} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex-7) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=7} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex-8) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=8} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex-9) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=9} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex-10) ::: :::
## Geometric growth with env. stochasticity ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} $$ r_t \sim \mbox{Normal}(\bar{r}=0.1, \sigma^2=0.25) $$ ::: ::: {.cell} :::
::: {.r-stack} ::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex2-1) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex2-2) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex2-3) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex2-4) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex2-5) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=5} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex2-6) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=6} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex2-7) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=7} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex2-8) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=8} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex2-9) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=9} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/geo-env-ex2-10) ::: :::
## Logistic growth with environmental stochasticity
Imagine the carrying capacity fluctuates randomly.
$$ N_{t+1} = N_t + N_tr_{max}(1 - N_t/K_t) \\ K_t \sim \mbox{Normal}(\bar{K}, \sigma^2) $$ ## Logistic example with environmental stochasticity ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} $$ K_t \sim \mbox{Normal}(\bar{K}=200, \sigma^2=50) $$ ::: ::: {.cell} :::
::: {.r-stack} ::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/logistic-ex-1) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/logistic-ex-2) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/logistic-ex-3) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/logistic-ex-4) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/logistic-ex-5) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=5} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/logistic-ex-6) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=6} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/logistic-ex-7) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=7} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/logistic-ex-8) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=8} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/logistic-ex-9) ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=9} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/logistic-ex-10) ::: :::
# Demographic stochasticity {visibility="hidden"} ## Demographic stochasticity ::: {style='font-size: 80%;'} We can make the BIDE model stochastic by modeling random variation in the number of individuals that are born and die each year (we'll ignore movement): $$ N_{t+1} = N_t + B_t - D_t $$
::: {.fragment} What distributions should we use for $B_t$ and $D_t$? ::: ::: {.fragment} $$ B_t \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(N_t\times b) $$ $$ D_t \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N_t, d) $$ ::: ::: ## Poisson distribution ::: {style='font-size: 90%;'} The Poisson distribution is useful for data that are non-negative integers.
It has a single parameter that describes the expected value of the random outcomes.
::: {.fragment} In stochastic population models, the Poisson distribution can be used to model the number of births ($B_t$) that occur in a time interval. $$ B_t \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(N_t \times b) $$ ::: ::: ## Poisson distributions ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/pois-1.png){fig-align='center' width=0.9
textwidth} ::: ::: ## Binomial distribution The binomial distribution is also useful for data that are non-negative integers, but it has an upper bound.
::: {.fragment} In population models, the upper bound is often population size, and we use the model to describe how many individuals die during some time period.
$$ D_t \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N_t, d) $$ ::: ## Binomial distributions ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/bin-1.png){fig-align='center' width=0.9
textwidth} ::: ::: ## Demographic stochasticity ::: {style='font-size: 70%;'} Poisson-Binomial birth-death model. $$ \begin{gather*} N_{t+1} = N_t + B_t - D_t \\ B_t \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(N_t \times b) \\ D_t \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N_t, d) \end{gather*} $$ ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lecture-stochasticity_files/figure-revealjs/pois-bin-1.png){fig-align='center' width=0.7
textwidth} ::: ::: ## Summary
Purely deterministic models are too rigid.
Purely stochastic models don't describe population processes.
The goal is to develop mechanistic models that represent our biological understanding while allowing for uncertainty.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
